interest: This file offers valuable insight into the intersection of post-war Japanese macroeconomic stabilization, coalition politics under Prime Minister Tetsu Katayama, and international financial diplomacy during the Allied Occupation. It illuminates how Bank of Japan officials actively briefed American occupation authorities to resist radical economic proposals from the Social Democratic Party's left wing, framing the proposed cancellation of war bond interest as a covert attempt to force private banking insolvency and nationalization. Concurrently, the British diplomatic reporting highlights the early international pressures surrounding Japan's pre-war external debt, illustrating how Allied creditors sought to safeguard bondholders' rights in the upcoming peace treaty negotiations while recognizing Japan's precarious post-war balance of payments.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.5161, covering February 2 to February 13, 1948) concerns post-World War II financial conditions, public debt, and banking policy in Japan, specifically addressing interest payments on domestic war bonds and foreign debt service. It includes a despatch from W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser in Tokyo, enclosing a detailed memorandum of conversation with Shigeo Matsumoto, secretary to the Governor of the Bank of Japan, which warns that discontinuing domestic war bond interest would inflict a five-billion-yen annual loss on commercial banks, undermine anti-inflation savings drives, burden industrial production, and potentially serve as a pretext for bank nationalization advocated by leftist Social Democrats. In addition, the file contains an airgram from the American Embassy in London transcribing a House of Commons exchange between MP Edward Keeling and Chancellor of the Exchequer Sir Stafford Cripps regarding the protection of British bondholders' rights and the prospects for Japan resuming service on its external debt in future peace treaty negotiations.

subfiles.about: Reports on the financial and political implications in Japan of proposals to discontinue or reduce interest payments on domestic war bonds.
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald (Acting Political Adviser, Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Acting Political Adviser W. J. Sebald forwards a report and memorandum of conversation concerning Prime Minister Tetsu Katayama's remarks on war bond interest. Drawing on consultations with Shigeo Matsumoto of the Bank of Japan, Sebald notes that canceling interest on war bonds would cost Japanese commercial banks five billion yen annually, jeopardizing national savings campaigns or severely penalizing industrial borrowers. Minister of Labor Mitsusuke Yonekubo indicated that the Cabinet was exploring reducing the interest rate to one percent rather than outright elimination, although coalition partners in the Democratic and People's Cooperative parties were expected to resist even that compromise.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 67 from Tokyo on Effect of Discontinuance of Payment of Interest on War Bonds

subfiles.about: Records conversations with Shigeo Matsumoto of the Bank of Japan regarding the quantitative impacts and political motives surrounding war bond interest cancellation.
subfiles.from: W. Henry Lawrence, Jr. (Second Secretary of Mission)
subfiles.summary: Second Secretary W. Henry Lawrence, Jr. records discussions held with Shigeo Matsumoto, secretary to Bank of Japan Governor Hisato Ichimada, on January 20 and 22, 1948. Matsumoto explained that out of roughly 20 billion yen in war bonds bearing 3.5% interest (7 billion yen annually), 70% were held by banking institutions and 10-15% by the Bank of Japan. He pointed out that private banks could not absorb the loss without either lowering deposit rates—which would sabotage the campaign to boost savings and curb inflation—or raising commercial loan rates, thereby crippling industrial production. Matsumoto asserted that leftist agitation within the Social Democratic Party to halt interest payments was a calculated strategy to destabilize the banking sector and justify state nationalization.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Effect of Discontinuance of Payment of Interest on War Bonds
subfiles.to: Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan

subfiles.about: Transmits a British parliamentary question and answer from Hansard on the resumption of service on Japanese external debt.
subfiles.summary: The American Embassy in London transmits an excerpt from the House of Commons debates (Hansard) of February 3, 1948, concerning Japanese bonds. Member of Parliament Edward Keeling questioned Chancellor of the Exchequer Sir Stafford Cripps on whether the British Government would support American initiatives to resume service on Japanese bonds and what Japanese intentions were. Sir Stafford Cripps answered that while bondholders' rights would be considered during future peace treaty discussions, Japan's balance-of-payments situation made the resumption of external debt service unlikely in the near future.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-312 from London on Resumption of Service on Japanese Bonds
